newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary slams OECD plans to free land sales.
newsitem.headline: Hungary slams OECD plans to free land sales.

text.p: Hungary wants to protect domestic land and real estate owners by opposing liberal sales rules plans within the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the Finance Ministry said on Thursday.
"Land prices are very low in Hungary," OECD workgroup head Agnes Vargha told a news conference held on the occasion of the first anniversary of Hungary's joining the OECD.
"Hungarian land would be too easy prey to (foreign) institutional investors," she said.

She said that a liberalisation in the next few years would be difficult as land ownership in Hungary has been muddled by the privatisation of land to masses of individuals and because Hungary is only preparing the regulation of mortgages.
Hungary has already liberalised all current account deals as a condition of joining the OECD and will continue to remove remaining barriers to capital movements, Vargha added.

The government plans to submit by August a package of law amendments to Parliament, aiming at allowing foreign companies to set up branches in the country from January 1, 1998, department head Annamaria Ivanics told Reuters.
This liberalisation step is seen generating sharp competition in many sectors of the economy, including financial services.
The last stage of the liberalisation process will be the freeing of short-term capital movements towards the end of the century, Vargha said.
Currently foreigners can only buy Hungarian securities with a minimum one year maturity.
She added that Hungary would join a planned multilateral Agreement on Investment of OECD countries.

The agreement, the framework of which is likely to be finalised this year, is aimed at setting up the obligatory liberalisation minimum of international investment for OECD members, and lift further barriers, Vargha said.

However, Hungary has some reservations concerning possible compulsory liberalisation, such as plans to free land and real estate purchases for foreigners and strengthening their participation in transportation, she said.
She added that Hungary will not be alone with its objections as other OECD countries shared them.
These objections did not mean that Hungary was dissatisfied with its OECD membership as such.

Joining the OECD in March 1996 helped Hungary to improve its international recognition substantially and getting investment grades from international credit rating agencies last year, Finance Ministry officials said.
